entries.speaker: Enrico Fermi
entries.quote: It [the Schrodinger equation] has no business being that good, you know, Stan.
entries.work: quoted in Stanislaw M. Ulam, Adventures of a Mathematician (New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, 1976), Part III, "Los Alamos"
entries.date: 1976 (book); the exchange is dated by Ulam to after the war
entries.context: On a downhill walk in Frijoles Canyon after the war. Ulam had told Fermi that in his last year of high school he read popular accounts of Heisenberg, Schrodinger and De Broglie, learned that solving the Schrodinger equation gives hydrogen levels to six decimals, and wondered "how such an artificially abstracted equation could work to better than one part in a million. A partial differential equation pulled out of thin air, it seemed to me, despite the appearances of derivation by analogies." The bracketed gloss "[the Schrodinger equation]" is Ulam's, as printed.
entries.caution: Transcribed from the scanned Scribner 1976 printing held in the private repository; the PDF carries no text layer and the text was obtained by Tesseract OCR at 200 dpi (PDF page 170) and read back against the page image. Printed page number taken from the running footer (165). The printing spells 'Schrodinger' without the umlaut throughout this passage. EXHIBIT_report.md note 74 cites pp. 165-166 for this and the following remark from the 1991 University of California Press reprint; the Scribner 1976 printing carries the same pagination, verified against the running footers.

entries.speaker: Enrico Fermi
entries.quote: No, I didn't succeed to my satisfaction in giving a really rational introduction to quantum theory.
entries.work: quoted in Stanislaw M. Ulam, Adventures of a Mathematician (New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, 1976), Part III, "Los Alamos"
entries.date: 1976 (book); reported of the summer following the Frijoles Canyon walk
entries.context: Immediately follows the Frijoles Canyon exchange. Fermi "went on to say that in the fall he intended to give a really logical introduction and derivation of quantum theory in his course at the University of Chicago. He apparently worked at it, but told me the next summer, when he returned to Los Alamos" — then this sentence. Ulam's own comment follows: "It is not just a question of axioms as some naive purist might think. The question is why such and no other axiom? Any working algorithm can be axiomatized."
entries.caution: Transcribed from the scanned Scribner 1976 printing by OCR at 200 dpi (PDF page 171) and read back against the page image. Printed page number from the running footer (166). OCR rendered the opening double quotation mark as a doubled mark and broke 'satisfaction' across the line as 'satisfac-tion'; both repaired against the page image. Note that Fermi says 'logical' when stating the intention and 'rational' when reporting the failure; both readings are as printed.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: Somehow he seemed the embodiment of wisdom. (Wisdom, perhaps not genius in the sense of Newton or Einstein.) He knew what not to attempt and how much could be done without mathematics, which he left to others. This enormous wisdom is what I liked about him.
entries.work: Stanislaw M. Ulam, Adventures of a Mathematician (New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, 1976), Part III, "Los Alamos"
entries.context: Ulam on Niels Bohr, who "was in Los Alamos for several months": "He was not very old. To me at thirty-five, he seemed ancient, even though Bohr in his late fifties was very active and energetic, physically as well as mentally. He walked, skied, and hiked in the Los Alamos mountains." This is the paragraph of praise that precedes the criticism of complementarity.
entries.caution: Transcribed from the scanned Scribner 1976 printing by OCR at 200 dpi (PDF page 172) and read back against the page image. Printed page number from the running footer (167). The parentheses around the second sentence are as printed.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: Departing from his usual caution about expressing opinions about other people, Fermi remarked once that when Bohr talked he sometimes gave the impression of a Catholic priest celebrating mass. It was an iconoclastic statement, since so many physicists are still under the spell of Bohr.
entries.work: Stanislaw M. Ulam, Adventures of a Mathematician (New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, 1976), Part III, "Los Alamos"
entries.context: Stands as its own paragraph between Ulam's praise of Bohr's wisdom (p. 167) and his criticism of complementarity (pp. 167-168). Fermi's remark is reported by Ulam in indirect speech, not quoted.
entries.caution: Transcribed from the scanned Scribner 1976 printing by OCR at 200 dpi (PDF page 172) and read back against the page image. Printed page number from the running footer (167). The printing reads 'It was an iconoclastic statement'; EXHIBIT_report.md renders the same clause as Ulam calling this 'an iconoclastic statement, since so many physicists are still under the spell of Bohr,' which adapts the leading pronoun to the reporting sentence. Fermi's remark itself is Ulam's indirect report and carries no quotation marks in the printing.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: He had his own kind of genius that made him a great physicist but, to my mind, some of his students were almost benighted by his complementarity philosophy of "one can say this, but on the other hand one can. . ." or "one cannot say sharply what this means." People without his great sense and intuitive wisdom were led astray and lost the precision and sharpness of their intellectual or scientific approach, in my opinion. But he still has many admirers. Victor F. Weisskopf is one. It seems to me that as a philosophical guideline, complementarity is essentially negative. It can only console. Whether it can be positively useful other than in philosophical consolations is a question which troubles me.
entries.work: Stanislaw M. Ulam, Adventures of a Mathematician (New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, 1976), Part III, "Los Alamos"
entries.context: Ulam's own position on complementarity, following the paragraph of praise for Bohr personally and the reported Fermi remark. The passage spans a page break: it begins at the foot of p. 167 ('He had his own kind of genius...') and continues on p. 168. The last three sentences ('It seems to me...troubles me.') are a separate paragraph in the printing.
entries.caution: Transcribed from the scanned Scribner 1976 printing by OCR at 200 dpi (PDF pages 172-173) and read back against the page images. Printed page numbers from the running footers (167), (168). The suspension points inside the first inner quotation are set as '. . .' in the printing and are Bohr's manner of speaking as Ulam renders it, not an editorial elision. EXHIBIT_report.md quotes this passage with a marked ellipsis in place of 'But he still has many admirers. Victor F. Weisskopf is one.'; the full text is carried here so that elision can be checked.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: Bohr's speech was very difficult to understand, and anecdotes about him abound. Most of the time it was impossible to get his exact words.
entries.work: Stanislaw M. Ulam, Adventures of a Mathematician (New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, 1976), Part III, "Los Alamos"
entries.context: Opens the run of Bohr anecdotes that follows the complementarity passage: the Ruby Scherr 'Guess how much?' story, Bohr's wartime pseudonym Nicholas Baker, and Weisskopf's slip at the colloquium.
entries.caution: Transcribed from the scanned Scribner 1976 printing by OCR at 200 dpi (PDF page 173) and read back against the page image. Printed page number from the running footer (168). EXHIBIT_report.md note 74 quotes this with a marked ellipsis as 'Bohr's speech was very difficult to understand ... Most of the time it was impossible to get his exact words.'; the elided words are 'and anecdotes about him abound.'
